subject: Overlay network controls and fail-open scenarios — architecture Q&A

Subject: Redwood overlay controls + fail-open behavior — quick Qs

Naomi,

Thanks again for taking the time on Friday. Crescent has a couple of architecture questions we need to close in the RFP: specifically around your overlay network between inference workers and the control plane, and how Redwood handles fail-open scenarios for sidecar proxies and key material access. High level asks below — a short narrative and any diagrams would be great.

1) How is the overlay network segmented between customers (logical per-tenant overlay vs shared overlay)? What controls enforce tenant separation at L2/L3?
2) If a sidecar proxy or control-plane route fails, under what conditions do you allow traffic to fall back (fail-open) versus failing closed? Any automatic fallback heuristics?
3) Evidence: a simple diagram showing the overlay boundary, bastion/egress points, and any ACL enforcement points.

We’re on a tight timeline — can you get responses and a diagram by Wednesday EOD PT?

Appreciate it,
Tom

Tom Adler
Head of Security Architecture
Crescent Bank
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi.feldman@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Redwood overlay controls + fail-open behavior — quick Qs

Tom —

Thanks for the clear list. We can get you a concise narrative plus an annotated topology by Wednesday. Quick answers up front so your reviewers have context while we finalize the diagram:

1) Tenant segmentation: Redwood runs a layered isolation model. Each tenant gets a logical overlay namespace implemented by mutually authenticated mTLS tunnels anchored at tenant-specific sidecars. Control-plane sidecar policies and dataplane ACLs (implemented at the virtual switch and host iptables level) enforce L3 scoping; heavy-tenancy customers may opt into dedicated overlay namespaces backed by isolated VPC segments in their region (Dedicated/Private offerings).

2) Fail-open behavior: by default, we favor fail-closed for any flow that would expose customer data or control-plane credentials. Fail-open is only allowed for non-sensitive inference caching or telemetry paths and only when an explicit policy allows lenient fallback. Heuristics:
  - Control-plane auth failure (e.g., KMS unreachable): fail-closed for request tokens and model pulls; we return a 503 with safe error.
  - Sidecar proxy lost route to KV cache: if the request does not require cached secrets and the model is pinned locally, sidecar may serve from local cache (graceful degrade).
  - Egress gateway loss: if egress is required for external fetch (3rd-party logging), we queue and backpressure rather than open an alternate path.

3) Diagram: attaching an annotated overlay topology and a short mitigation checklist.

Attaching: redwood_overlay_topology_v2.png; failopen-mitigation-checklist.pdf

I’ll loop in Jonas and Irene for a short technical note on the exact ACL enforcement points and a text extract of the egress policy for your audit pack (Jonas — can you add the egress policy snippet I promised?).

Best,

Naomi — adding the technical extract you can include in the packet. Paste below and I attached the short text file with the iptable/eBPF enforcement points.

--- technical extract start ---
Overlay enforcement points (concise):
- Tenant overlay namespace created per deployment via our orchestration layer (namespace id bound to tenant id).
- Sidecar-to-sidecar communication is mTLS (SPIFFE-style identities). Only identities bound to the same tenant namespace are allowed to exchange inference traffic; control-plane RPCs require a cross-namespace role binding where explicitly allowed.
- Host-level enforcement: we enforce L3/L4 rules via eBPF programs pinned at the ingress device; these map overlay namespace IDs to cgroups and drop any cross-namespace flows unless an allowlist policy exists.
- Egress gating: all outbound connections from the inference nodes are funneled through a per-region egress gateway that performs destination allowlist checks and TLS inspection metadata tagging (no plaintext capture).

Fail-open policy summary (concise):
- Default: fail-closed for auth and disk/key access.
- Controlled fail-open allowed for read-only cache hits for models and for telemetry-forwarding buffer drains; requires explicit tenant opt-in via account configuration and a documented risk acceptance.
- Automated detection: the runtime evaluates three signals (auth error rate, sidecar health percentage, and KV response latency). If all three exceed thresholds, runtime rejects new requests requiring fresh secrets and returns 503; background syncs continue to attempt recovery.

Audit evidence extract: see attached egress-policy-extract.txt (snippet of our outbound gating rules and allowlist examples).
--- technical extract end ---

Let me know if you want a small snippet that shows the eBPF match rule for overlay IDs — I can include a sanitized example.

—Jonas

Tom —

Attached are the consolidated artifacts you requested for the security RFP: an annotated overlay topology, a short mitigation checklist showing our decision logic for fail-open vs fail-closed, and an extract of the egress gating rules for your audit team. Highlights in plain language:

- Isolation model: logical overlay per-tenant with eBPF/iptables host enforcement and mTLS between sidecars. Customers on Dedicated/Private can opt for VPC-backed overlay isolation.
- Fail-open posture: default fail-closed for auth/key retrieval and model pulls. Fail-open only for non-sensitive cache/telemetry and only with explicit tenant opt-in. Automatic heuristics ensure the runtime rejects risky requests during degraded auth states.
- Evidence: redwood_overlay_topology_v2.png, failopen-mitigation-checklist.pdf, egress-policy-extract.txt.
